What is Angular? A Beginner's Introducti: Angular = a framework from Google for building web apps in TypeScript.
You build the screen from components: a class, a template and styles.
Routing, forms, HTTP and testing tools come in one place.
When data changes, Angular updates only the parts of the page that need it.
TypeScript Basics for Angular: TypeScript = JavaScript with types. You say what kind of value a variable or function holds.
The editor and compiler check types while you type, so mistakes show up early.
Most used in Angular: interfaces, classes and decorators.
It is turned into plain JavaScript for the browser.
Install Node.js and the Angular CLI: Install Node.js first. Angular tools run on it.
npm comes with Node and installs packages.
Angular Course Roadmap and Complete Topi: Path: basics, then state and forms, then routing and HTTP, then advanced topics, then projects and deploy.
State = signals and services. Real data = routing and HTTP.
Advanced = RxJS, change detection, SSR, testing, security.
Create Your First Angular App with the C: `ng new my-app` creates a complete project.
`cd my-app` then `ng serve` starts the dev server.
Save a file and the browser reloads by itself.
Angular Project Structure Explained: `main.ts` is the entry point and starts the app.
The root component holds the page layout.
`app.routes.ts` says which component shows for each URL.
Everything is drawn inside `index.html`, the one page the browser loads.
Your First Angular Component: A component = a class with a `@Component` decorator.
The template is HTML that shows data from the class. Styles apply only to this component.
`selector` is the custom tag name, for example `<app-card>`.
Put the tag in another template and Angular draws the component there.
Make one with `ng generate component name`.
Angular CLI Guide: ng new, ng update, Mu: The Angular CLI is one tool for the whole life of a project.
`ng new` creates, `ng serve` runs, `ng build` makes the files to deploy.
`ng generate` makes components, services and more with the right files.
`ng update` upgrades Angular and runs migrations on your code.
Upgrade one major version at a time.
Displaying Data in Angular with Interpol: Interpolation: `{{ title }}` shows a class property in the template.
When the property changes, the text updates.
Small expressions work inside the braces, such as `{{ price * 2 }}`.
Keep logic short in templates. Move bigger logic to the class.
Property Binding and Event Binding in An: Property binding: `[disabled]="isBusy"` sets an element property from the class.
Event binding: `(click)="save()"` runs a method when the event happens.
Square brackets = data in. Round brackets = events out.
The method changes the data and the bindings update the screen.
Angular Two-Way Binding: ngModel, ngMode: Two-way binding keeps a property and an input in sync in both directions.
Anything else that shows `name` updates as the user types.
Angular Signals: Reactive State for Begi: A signal holds a value and tells Angular when it changes.
Angular knows which parts of the page read the signal and refreshes only those.
Update signals with new objects and arrays, not by changing them in place.
Angular Styling: Global Styles, Componen: `styles.css` = global styles for the whole app.
Component styles apply only to that component.
View encapsulation is how Angular stops a component's styles leaking out.
Libraries such as Bootstrap and Font Awesome are added once and used through classes.
Conditional Rendering in Angular with @i: `@if (cond) { ... } @else { ... }` decides which blocks exist on the page.
Only the matching block is added. The other is not in the page at all.
Control flow is built in. No import is needed.
Rendering Lists in Angular with @for and: `@for (item of items; track item.id) { ... }` repeats a block for each item.
`track` tells Angular which item is which. Use a unique id.
Angular then adds, moves or removes only what changed.
`@empty { ... }` shows something when the list is empty.
Angular ngIf, ngFor, ngSwitch and trackB: Older code uses `*ngIf`, `*ngFor`, `*ngSwitch` and `trackBy`. You will still meet them.
The new `@if`, `@for` and `@switch` do the same job with less code.
A built-in migration converts templates for you: `ng generate @angular/core:control-flow`.
Review the changes and run your tests.
Angular ngClass, ngStyle, Class Binding: A class binding adds or removes one class: `[class.active]="isActive"`.
`ngClass` handles several classes from an object or a list.
A style binding sets one property: `[style.width.px]="size"`.
The element updates whenever the state changes.
Computed Signals and Effects in Angular: `computed(() => price() * qty())` calculates a value from other signals.
It recalculates only when those signals change, and is cached until then.
`effect(() => ...)` runs code when the signals it reads change.
Use effects for logging or saving to storage, not to calculate values.
Signals in Practice: Build a Shopping Ca: The cart keeps its lines in one signal.
Item count and total are `computed` signals that read the lines.
The cart view refreshes with no extra code.
Angular Component Inputs: Pass Data to C: A parent gives data to a child with an input: `[product]="item"`.
In the child: `product = input.required<Product>()`. Read it with `product()`.
Data flows one way, from parent to child.
When the parent value changes, the child updates.
Angular Component Outputs and Two-Way Bi: A child tells its parent with an output: `saved = output<string>()`, then `saved.emit(value)`.
`model()` combines an input and an output, so the child can change a value the parent owns.
Angular Pipes: Format Dates, Currency an: A pipe changes how a value is shown, not the value itself.
`{{ value | pipeName }}`. Add options with a colon: `date:'dd MMM yyyy'`.
Angular Built-in Pipes: Date, Async, Key: The `async` pipe subscribes to an observable or promise and shows its latest value.
It unsubscribes when the component is destroyed, so you cannot forget.
`keyvalue` loops over the keys and values of an object.
In TypeScript, inject the pipe or create it and call `transform`.
Angular Lifecycle Hooks: OnInit, OnDestr: A component is created, updates, then is removed. Hooks let you run code at each stage.
`ngOnInit` runs once after inputs are set: load initial data here.
`ngAfterViewInit` runs once the view and children exist.
`ngOnDestroy` runs just before removal: stop timers and subscriptions.
Template Reference Variables, ng-contain: `#box` gives a name to an element in the template.
`viewChild()` gets something inside the component's own template.
`contentChild()` gets something the parent projected in.
`ng-container` groups elements or holds an `@if` without adding an extra element.
Angular Services and Dependency Injectio: A service = a class that holds logic or data you want to reuse, such as API calls.
A component asks for it with `inject(MyService)`. It does not use `new`.
Every component gets the same instance.
Components stay small and services are easy to replace in tests.
Share State Between Components with an A: Two unrelated components that need the same data: put the data in a service.
The service is one shared instance and keeps the state in a signal.
Component A calls a service method to change it.
Component B reads the signal and updates by itself.
Angular Hierarchical Dependency Injectio: Angular has a tree of injectors that follows the component tree.
A request looks in the component's own providers, then the parent, then the root.
A provider on a component gives that branch its own instance.
`@Self` = only here. `@SkipSelf` = start at the parent. `@Optional` = no error if missing. `@Host` = stop at the host.
Angular Reactive Forms for Beginners: Reactive form: you build the model in the class. `FormGroup` holds a `FormControl` per field.
The model always has the current values.
On submit read `form.value` and send it.
Angular Form Validation: Built-in and Cu: Validators are rules a control must satisfy: `required`, `minLength`, `email`.
Angular checks them on each change and sets the status.
Show an error only when the control is invalid and touched.
A custom validator is a function that returns an error object, or `null` when valid.
Angular Template-Driven Forms with ngMod: Template-driven form: most of the setup is in the HTML.
Add `ngModel` and a `name` to each input.
Use HTML attributes like `required` for validation.
FormControl, FormGroup, FormBuilder, set: `FormControl` = one field. `FormGroup` = a group of fields. `FormBuilder` = shorter way to create them.
`setValue` needs every field. `patchValue` updates only some.
`valueChanges` emits on each change. `statusChanges` emits when valid or invalid changes.
Unsubscribe or use `takeUntilDestroyed` when you listen manually.
Angular Forms: Select Dropdowns, Checkbo: Select and radio groups store one chosen value. A checkbox stores `true` or `false`.
Typed forms know the type of each control, so mistakes show in the editor.
`FormRecord` is for groups where the keys are not known in advance.
Angular Advanced Form Validation: Custom: Custom validators encode your rules, such as a password policy.
Async validators wait for a result (is the username taken?). The control is `pending` meanwhile.
A cross-field validator sits on the group and compares fields, like password and confirm.
`setValidators` changes rules at runtime. Then call `updateValueAndValidity()`.
Angular Routing Basics: Pages, RouterLin: Routing shows different pages for different URLs without a full reload.
Routes are listed in `app.routes.ts`: a `path` and a `component`.
`<router-outlet />` marks where the page is drawn.
Angular Route Parameters and Query Param: Route parameter: required part of the path, `/products/:id`.
Query parameter: optional, after the `?`, like `?sort=price&page=2`.
The component reads both and loads the right data.
`withComponentInputBinding()` lets route params arrive as inputs.
Angular Router Navigation: ActivatedRout: `routerLink` for links in a template. `router.navigate([...])` when code decides, for example after saving.
`ActivatedRoute` gives params, query params and route data.
Router events tell you when navigation starts and ends. Use them for loading bars.
Angular Route Guards: Protect Pages with: A guard is a function that decides whether a route may open: `canActivate: [authGuard]`.
Return `true` to open, or a redirect (`router.parseUrl('/login')`).
The server must still check permissions. A guard only hides pages.
Angular Guards: CanActivateChild, CanDea: `canActivateChild` protects all children of a route.
`canDeactivate` runs before leaving: warn about unsaved changes.
`resolve` fetches data before the page shows.
`canMatch` decides whether a route applies at all, for example by role.
Preloading can fetch lazy routes in the background.
Angular Lazy Loading: Load Routes and Co: Without lazy loading the first download holds the whole app.
A lazy route is split into its own file: `loadComponent: () => import('./page').then(m => m.Page)`.
The file downloads only when the user opens the route. `loadChildren` does it for a group of routes.
The first load stays small and fast.
Angular HttpClient: Get Data from an API: Keep API calls in a service, not in the component.
Add `provideHttpClient()` in the app config. Then `inject(HttpClient)`.
`http.get<T>(url)` returns an observable. Nothing is sent until someone subscribes.
Subscribe, or use the `async` pipe, and show the data.
Angular HTTP: Loading State, Error Handl: Set a loading flag before the request so the user sees something is happening.
`http.post(url, body)` sends data as the request body.
On success turn off loading and update the screen.
On failure catch the error and show a clear message, not a blank screen.
Angular HTTP: Query Parameters, Headers,: One service can cover every action your API supports.
`HttpParams` or `{ params: { page: 2 } }` for query parameters. Headers for tokens and content type.
PUT replaces a whole item. PATCH changes only some fields. DELETE removes an item by id.
Each call returns an observable of the result.
RxJS Basics for Angular: Observables and: An observable = a stream of values over time (clicks, HTTP results).
Operators are small steps added with `pipe()`: `map` changes each value, `filter` keeps some.
Unsubscribe when done, or let the `async` pipe do it.
RxJS Observables Explained: Create from: `of(1, 2, 3)` emits the values you give, then completes.
`from([..])` turns an array, string or promise into a stream.
`fromEvent(el, 'click')` turns browser events into a stream.
RxJS take, takeUntil, takeWhile, first,: `skip(n)` ignores the first values. `take(n)` stops after n values.
`tap` looks at values, for logging, without changing them.
`takeUntil(destroy$)` is a common way to clean up.
RxJS scan, reduce, debounceTime, debounc: `debounceTime(400)` waits until typing stops: one API call instead of one per key.
`scan` keeps a running result and emits it for every value, like a live total.
`reduce` emits only the final result, when the stream completes.
`delay` and `delayWhen` shift values later in time.
RxJS Error Handling: throwError, catchEr: An error ends an observable unless you handle it.
`retry(3)` tries again a set number of times.
`catchError` lets you recover: return a fallback with `of(...)`, or `throwError` to pass on a clearer error.
`finalize` runs at the end either way: a good place to hide a spinner.
RxJS Subjects in Angular: Subject, Behav: A subject is an observable you can also push values into with `next()`.
`BehaviorSubject` keeps the latest value, so new subscribers get it at once.
`AsyncSubject` gives only the last value, on completion.
Prefer signals for simple shared state in new code.
Test Angular Components and Services wit: A test: set up, do something, check the result.
`TestBed` creates the component with the same setup the app uses.
Change inputs or click a button, then let Angular update with `fixture.detectChanges()`.
Use `expect` to check text or values. Vitest runs the file.
For services, mock the HTTP calls.
Angular Accessibility: Build Apps Everyo: Accessibility = people with different needs can use your app.
Use the right HTML: real buttons, links, labels and headings.
ARIA only where plain HTML cannot say it.
Everything must work with the keyboard, with a visible focus.
Manage focus when the page changes so screen reader users know where they are.
Angular Performance and Production Build: A production build minifies and removes unused code: `ng build`.
Lazy loading keeps the first download small.
Check bundle sizes and measure with Lighthouse.
Angular Project 1: Build a Task Manager: Task manager: add form, list, toggle and delete, filter (all, active, done).
A service keeps all tasks in one signal.
A computed signal gives the filtered list.
Angular Project 2: Employee Management D: Employee dashboard: list, detail page and edit form.
A service talks to the API for all employee data.
The table page has search and sorting.
A reactive form with validators adds or edits an employee.
Routes connect the pages. A guard can protect the edit screens.
Angular Project 3: Online Learning Platf: Capstone: login with a guard, token sent with requests.
Courses load from an API on lazy routes.
A lesson page reads its id from the route.
Progress is kept in signals and saved back to the API.
Deploy an Angular App: Netlify, Firebase: `ng build` creates the production files in `dist`.
Upload `dist` to Netlify, Firebase Hosting or your own Nginx server.
The host must send `index.html` for unknown paths, or refreshing a deep link gives a 404.
Angular effect() and linkedSignal(): Adv: `linkedSignal` = a writable signal derived from another signal.
When the source changes it resets to a new default. You can still `set` it yourself.
`effect()` reruns when the signals it reads change.
Use effect for side effects, such as saving to storage. Not for computing values.
Angular resource() and httpResource(): S: `httpResource` loads data from an API and exposes it as signals.
It watches a request signal, such as an id, and sends a new request when it changes.
`resource()` works the same way for any async source.
Check the current docs, these APIs are newer and may change.
Angular Custom Directives: Attribute Dir: A directive adds behaviour to an existing element. It has no template.
The `host` property binds classes and styles and listens to events on that element.
Angular Content Projection: ng-content,: Content projection: a parent puts its own HTML inside a component.
The component marks a spot with `<ng-content />`.
The parent writes content between the component tags.
`ng-template` holds markup that is drawn only when `ngTemplateOutlet` renders it.
Angular Dynamic Components and Host Dire: Dynamic component = chosen at runtime, such as in a dialog.
Host directives let a component apply a directive's behaviour to itself, with no extra template code.
Angular ElementRef, Renderer2, HostBindi: `ElementRef` gives a handle on the element itself.
Prefer `Renderer2` to change it: safer and portable.
`@HostBinding` sets host properties. `@HostListener` listens for host events.
These decorators are the older style. Newer code uses the `host` metadata.
Angular Injection Tokens and Providers:: An injection token names a value that is not a class, such as a URL: `new InjectionToken<string>('API_URL')`.
A provider says which value the token gets: `{ provide: API_URL, useValue: '...' }`.
In tests, provide a different value or a fake class. The code does not change.
Angular HTTP Interceptors: Auth Tokens,: An interceptor sits between `HttpClient` and the network and sees every request and response.
Clone the request to add an auth token header.
Handle errors in one place, such as sending the user to login on a 401.
A counter in an interceptor can drive one global loading bar.
Angular Project Architecture: Features,: As an app grows, the folder layout matters more than any single file.
Group code by feature: orders, users, each with its own components and services.
`core` = app-wide services. `shared` = reusable components and pipes.
Features should not reach into each other. Share through core or shared.
Angular App Configuration, Environment V: Settings that differ between development and production go in configuration.
Provide them through `app.config.ts`, for example with an injection token.
`provideAppInitializer` runs a function before the app starts, such as loading remote settings.
Anything in a browser app is public. Never put secrets in it.
Angular Error Handling: Global ErrorHand: Provide a custom `ErrorHandler` to catch errors nobody else caught.
Send details to a logging service so you can fix them.
Show the user a short, friendly message, not a stack trace.
Handle expected HTTP errors close to the request. Let the global handler catch the rest.
Angular NgModules (Legacy), Module Routi: Older Angular apps group code into NgModules, with module routing and lazy modules.
New code uses standalone components that list their own `imports`.
Migration schematics convert modules to standalone step by step.
Angular Custom Form Controls with Contro: `ControlValueAccessor` lets your component act like a form input, for example a star rating.
`writeValue` receives the value from the form so the control can show it.
Call `onChange` to send a new value back. Call `onTouched` when touched.
The form then treats it like any other control, with validation.
Angular FormArray and Dynamic Forms: Add: A `FormArray` holds a list of controls, such as several phone numbers. It lives inside a `FormGroup`.
The template loops over the controls with `@for`.
Angular Signal Forms: Build Forms with S: Signal forms = a newer way to build forms based on signals.
Start with a signal holding your data as the model. The form is created from the model.
Each field exposes its state as signals: value, valid, touched.
This API is still evolving. Check the current docs before relying on it.
Angular State Management with a Signal S: A store = a service that keeps state in a private signal.
Components never change the state directly. They call methods on the store.
The store exposes read-only `computed` signals as selectors.
Views read the selectors and update automatically.
Advanced RxJS Patterns for Angular: Comb: `combineLatest` emits when any stream changes, with the latest value of each.
`switchMap` starts a request for that value and cancels the previous one if still running.
`share` or `shareReplay` lets many subscribers use one request.
Advanced Angular Routing: Resolvers, Chi: Child routes appear inside a layout's `<router-outlet />`.
A resolver fetches data before the page opens, so it never shows empty.
Preloading downloads lazy routes in the background after the first load.
View transitions can animate between pages when the browser supports it.
Angular Change Detection and Zoneless Ap: Change detection = how Angular finds out what to update on screen.
With zone.js, Angular is told after any async task and then checks components.
Signals tell Angular exactly which view depends on what, so less work is needed.
Zoneless apps do not need zone.js: signals and events trigger updates.
`OnPush` checks a component only when its inputs, events or signals change.
Angular Server-Side Rendering (SSR) and: A normal Angular app sends an almost empty page and builds the content in the browser.
SSR: the server runs Angular and sends full HTML, so people and search engines see content at once.
Hydration attaches Angular to the existing HTML so it becomes interactive without redrawing.
Angular SEO: Title, Meta Tags, Canonical: Set a unique title for every route with the `Title` service.
Use the `Meta` service for the description, and a canonical link.
SSR puts all of this in the HTML crawlers receive.
Lazy-load images below the fold and give them sizes.
Advanced Angular Testing: Guards, Interc: Test a guard with `runInInjectionContext` and check what it returns.
Test an interceptor with `HttpTestingController`: see the request, send a fake response.
The router testing harness navigates and lets you check which component showed.
Angular End-to-End Testing with Playwrig: An end-to-end test uses your app the way a user does.
Playwright opens a real browser, clicks and types, finding things by role and label.
Then it checks what appears on the screen.
Keep a few tests for the most important journeys: sign-up, checkout.
Angular Security Best Practices: XSS, To: Angular escapes values in templates, which protects against XSS. Avoid `bypassSecurityTrust...` unless you really must.
HttpOnly cookies are safer than local storage for tokens, but cookies need CSRF protection.
Set security headers such as `Content-Security-Policy` on your server.
The server must check every request.
Angular CI/CD with GitHub Actions: Test,: CI/CD runs your checks and deployment for you, every time.
A push starts the workflow: install, lint, test, build, deploy.
If a step fails, the later steps do not run.
Keep secrets in GitHub secrets, never in the repository.
Angular Troubleshooting: 404 on Refresh,: 404 on refresh: the server does not know Angular routes. Send `index.html` for unknown paths.
`ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenChecked`: a value changed after Angular checked it. Move the change earlier or use signals.
`EventTarget` typing errors: cast to the element you expect.
SSL on localhost: create and trust a local certificate for the dev server.
Read the error message, find the cause, fix that.
Angular Module Loaders: SystemJS, Webpac: A bundler turns many source files into files a browser can load.
Early Angular used SystemJS, then Webpack for many years.
Modern Angular builds with esbuild, and the dev server uses Vite. Both are much faster.
You still run `ng build` and `ng serve`.
Angular Advanced Capstone: Build and Shi: Plan the architecture first: features, routes, clear boundaries.
Add state with signals and load data over HTTP, with errors handled.
Test it. Check accessibility and security.
Add SSR and performance work. Let CI/CD ship it.

what-is-react-and-why-use-it: React = a JavaScript library for building screens out of small pieces called components.
You describe what the screen should look like for the current data. React does the updating.
Data flows down from parent to child. Changing data is called state.
Virtual DOM = a light copy of the page in memory. React compares old and new, then changes only the differences in the real page.
React is a library, not a full framework: you add routing, data fetching and so on yourself.
Learn basic HTML, CSS and JavaScript first. The lessons go in order.
set-up-react-with-vite-first-project: Vite = a fast development server and build tool. `npm run dev` starts it.
Create a project with `npm create vite@latest`, then `npm install`.
Browser loads `index.html`, which runs `main.jsx`, which draws `App` into the root div.
Edit and save: Vite updates the page at once, with no full reload.
Scripts in `package.json`: `dev` to work, `build` to make the final files, `preview` to try them.
If something fails, read the error in the terminal first. It usually names the file and line.
jsx-explained-simply: JSX looks like HTML but lives inside JavaScript. The browser cannot read it, so the build tool converts it.
Rule 1: return one parent element (or a fragment `<>...</>`).
Rule 2: close every tag, even `` and ``.
Components start with a capital letter. Styles are objects: `style={{ color: 'red' }}`.
react-components-and-props-explained: A component = a JavaScript function that returns JSX. Its name starts with a capital letter.
Props = the inputs of a component, like function arguments. The parent writes them like HTML attributes.
Destructure to keep it short: `function Greeting({ name, age })`. A default value: `{ label = 'Click me' }`.
Props are read-only. A child never changes its own props.
Text goes in quotes `name="Asha"`. Other values go in braces `age={24}`.
`children` = whatever you put between the opening and closing tags.
Never define a component inside another component.
react-usestate-hook-explained: A normal variable does not make the page redraw. State does.
`const [count, setCount] = useState(0);` gives the current value and a setter.
Calling the setter makes React call your component again with the new value.
Never change state directly. Use the setter, and make a new array or object instead of changing the old one.
State updates are not instant: the variable keeps its old value until the next draw.
Hooks go at the top level of a component, never inside `if`, loops or nested functions.
handling-events-in-react: Pass the function, do not call it: `onClick={handle}` not `onClick={handle()}`.
Need an argument? Wrap it: `onClick={() => remove(id)}`.
The event object `e` gives `e.target.value` for inputs. Use `e.preventDefault()` on form submit.
A child tells its parent by calling a function the parent passed as a prop.
Events bubble up from the child to its parents.
conditional-rendering-in-react: Four ways to show or hide: `if` before the return, ternary `a ? b : c`, `a && b`, or JSX saved in a variable.
A page that loads data has three screens: loading, error, and the data (or an empty message).
Return early for loading and error. It keeps the code flat.
With `&&`, make the left side a real true or false. `0 && ...` shows a 0 on the page.
Removing an element from the page is different from hiding it with CSS.
react-lists-and-keys-explained: `map` turns an array into a list of elements.
Every item needs a `key` that is unique and stable, usually the id from your data.
Never use a random key. Avoid the index when the list can be reordered.
Keys let React know which item is which, so it updates the right ones and keeps their state.
To change a list, make a new array with spread, filter or map. Never change the old one.
Show a friendly message when the list is empty.
react-forms-and-controlled-inputs: Controlled input = its value comes from state: `value={text} onChange={e => setText(e.target.value)}`.
State is the single source of truth, so the screen and the data never disagree.
Many fields: one state object and `setForm({ ...form, [name]: value })`.
Checkbox uses `checked` and `e.target.checked`. Select and textarea use `value`.
Validate on submit and show a clear message next to the field.
Clear the form after a good submit by setting the state back to its start value.
styling-react-apps-css-modules-tailwind: Plain CSS file: simple, but class names are global and can clash.
CSS Modules: each class gets a unique name, so styles stay inside one component.
Inline styles: `style={{ ... }}`. Good for values that change, not for everything.
Tailwind: small ready-made classes written straight in the JSX.
Design for phones first, then add rules for bigger screens.
react-useeffect-hook-explained: A side effect = work outside drawing: fetching data, timers, listeners.
React draws first, then runs the effect.
The dependency array decides when it runs: `[]` once, `[id]` when `id` changes, none after every draw.
Cleanup (the function you return) stops what you started: timers, listeners, requests.
In development, Strict Mode runs effects twice on purpose to find missing cleanup.
You might not need an effect: values you can work out while drawing do not need one.
fetch-data-in-react-loading-error-states: Every request has three states: loading, error, success.
Start the request in an effect, and pass an `AbortController` signal.
`fetch` does not throw on 404 or 500. Check `response.ok` yourself.
Cleanup aborts the old request, so old data cannot replace new data (the race condition).
Put repeated fetch code in one helper function.
react-useref-hook-dom-access: `useRef` makes a box with a `current` value that React keeps between draws.
Put `ref={myRef}` on an element and `myRef.current` is the real DOM element after drawing.
Common uses: focus an input, scroll to an element, keep a timer id, remember the previous value.
Changing a ref does not redraw the screen. If the screen must change, use state.
Use refs for things outside the data flow, not as a replacement for state.
lifting-state-up-and-component-compositi: Two components need the same value? Move the state to their closest shared parent.
Data goes down as props. Events go up as functions.
Only one copy of the data, so the parts can never disagree.
Derive values while drawing (like a total) instead of storing a second copy in state.
Passing props through many levels is tiring: use composition with `children`, or context.
Do not lift higher than needed. Keep state close to where it is used.
react-usereducer-hook-explained: `useReducer` is for state with many related changes.
The component sends an action: a small object such as `{ type: 'added', text }`.
`dispatch(action)` hands the current state and the action to the reducer.
The reducer returns a new state. It never changes the old one.
All the rules live in one place, so they are easy to read and test.
react-context-api-usecontext-explained: Context shares data with many components without passing props through every level.
Three steps: `createContext`, a `Provider` near the top with the `value`, and `useContext` where you need it.
Good for theme, signed-in user, language. Not for data that changes many times a second.
When the provider value changes, every component that reads it draws again.
Wrap `useContext` in a custom hook that throws a helpful error if the provider is missing.
Context is not a database. Keep server data in a data library.
react-custom-hooks-reuse-logic: A custom hook = a function whose name starts with `use` and that calls other hooks.
Same state and effect in two places? Move it into a hook, for example `useToggle` or `useLocalStorage`.
Hooks share logic, not data. Each component that calls the hook gets its own state.
Same rules as normal hooks: top level only, and only in components or other hooks.
Good hooks do one job, have a clear name, and return what the caller needs.
Improve the hook once and every component gets the improvement.
react-router-pages-links-navigation: `<Routes>` and `<Route path element>` decide which component shows for which address.
Use `<Link to>` instead of `<a>` so the page does not reload.
A layout route keeps the menu on screen and shows the page in `<Outlet />`.
`useNavigate` moves with code, for example after login.
Protected route = a wrapper that redirects when the user is not signed in. The server must still check.
A `*` route shows a not found page. Static hosts need a fallback to `index.html`.
react-forms-validation-formdata-react-ho: The browser already keeps form values. Give every input a `name`.
On submit: `new FormData(e.currentTarget)` reads all fields at once, so no state per field.
Your own validation function returns an object of errors. Show them next to the fields.
The server must always validate again. Browser checks can be skipped.
React Hook Form helps when a form is large or has many rules.
how-react-renders-rules-of-react-strictm: Render = React calls your component function to get JSX. It is not the same as changing the page.
A re-render starts with a state change, a parent render, or a changed context.
Components must be pure: same props and state give the same JSX. No changing outside values while rendering.
State is a snapshot. Replace objects and arrays, never change them.
Batching: many updates in one event give one render.
React commits only the real differences to the page.
`StrictMode` renders twice in development to help you find mistakes.
react-performance-memo-usememo-usecallba: Measure first with the React DevTools Profiler. Fix only what is really slow.
Simplest fix: move the state down into a small component.
`React.memo` skips a child when its props are the same.
`useMemo` keeps an expensive result. `useCallback` keeps a function steady.
Objects and functions are new on every render, which can break `memo`.
Long lists: show less, or virtualise. Do not search on every key press.
Do not add memo everywhere. It costs memory and makes code harder to read.
react-lazy-suspense-code-splitting: Code splitting = download code only when it is needed, so the first load is smaller.
`const Admin = lazy(() => import('./Admin'))` makes a separate file.
Wrap it in `<Suspense fallback={...}>` to show something while it loads.
Split by route first, then heavy libraries such as editors and charts.
Preload on hover or focus to hide the wait.
Check the result in the build output or the browser Network tab.
react-error-boundaries-portals-modals: An error while rendering can turn the whole page white. An error boundary catches it and shows a fallback.
Boundaries are class components (or a library). They need `getDerivedStateFromError` or `componentDidCatch`.
They do not catch errors in event handlers, fetch, timers or on the server.
Add a retry button and put boundaries around separate parts of the page.
A portal draws a component somewhere else in the DOM: `createPortal(jsx, document.body)`.
A good modal: `role="dialog"`, focus moves in, Escape closes, focus returns.
react-state-management-redux-toolkit-zus: Do you need a library? Only for client state shared by many far-apart components.
Redux flow: a component dispatches an action, the reducer returns new state, components read it with selectors.
Redux Toolkit makes this short with `createSlice`. Zustand does it with one `create` call.
Select only what you need so only those components redraw.
Never change state directly. Keep local state local.
Server data belongs in a data library such as TanStack Query.
tanstack-query-react-data-fetching: Server state is different from client state: it lives elsewhere, can be stale, and is shared.
The query key is the cache key. Include every value the request depends on.
Cached data shows at once. Stale data refreshes in the background.
`useMutation` changes data. Then `invalidateQueries` reloads the list.
Retries, cancelling and caching are built in, so you write less state code.
testing-react-vitest-testing-library: Test what the user sees and does, not the code inside.
Vitest runs the tests. React Testing Library draws the component in a fake browser.
Find elements the way people do: `getByRole`, `getByLabelText`, `getByText`.
`user-event` clicks and types like a real person. Then check with `expect`.
Components that use context or a router need to be wrapped in them in the test.
Good tests let you tidy code without breaking them.
react-accessibility-a11y-guide: Use the right HTML element: a real `button` works with keyboard and screen reader for free.
Label every field. Give meaningful images `alt` text.
Everything must work with the keyboard only. Keep the focus ring visible.
Do not use colour alone. Check contrast.
Use ARIA only when HTML is not enough. Live regions announce changes.
Test with the keyboard, Lighthouse or axe, and a screen reader. Tools find only part of the problems.
react-19-new-features-actions-use-optimi: Actions: pass a function to `<form action={fn}>`. React gives it the `FormData`.
`useActionState` keeps the result, the error and the pending flag.
`useFormStatus` lets a button know the form is sending.
`useOptimistic` shows the expected result at once. If the request fails, it goes back.
`use` can read a promise or context. `ref` is now a normal prop.
React Compiler and Server Components are bigger topics. Check what your tools support before you rely on them.
react-with-typescript-beginners-guide: Describe your data with a `type` or `interface`, such as `User`.
Type props: `function Card({ title }: { title: string })`.
Wrong or missing props show as a red line in the editor.
Types are removed at build time. They cannot check what the server really sends.
Avoid `any`. Read the first line of an error, it is usually the useful one.
react-project-structure-best-practices-d: Organise in clear folders and keep components small, with one job each.
Environment variables with `VITE_` are public. Never put secrets in React code.
Before shipping: test the real build, run Lighthouse, try the keyboard for a minute.
`npm run build` makes the `dist` folder of plain static files. Upload it to a host.
Turn on HTTPS and a fallback to `index.html` for React Router.
Client-only React is weak for SEO. Pages that must rank need server rendering or prerendering.
Next: build projects, then Next.js and a backend.

what-is-the-mern-stack: MERN = MongoDB (data), Express (API), React (screens), Node.js (runs JavaScript on the server).
A request: browser loads React, React calls the API with `fetch`, Express handles it, MongoDB returns documents, the data comes back as JSON.
One language, JavaScript, across the whole stack.
React shows, Express decides, MongoDB remembers.
set-up-your-tools-for-mern: Tools: an editor (VS Code), Node.js with npm, Git, and MongoDB (local or Atlas).
Node runs your code outside the browser. npm installs packages.
Git records every change so you can go back and share.
Keep projects in simple folders with no spaces in the names.
modern-javascript-for-mern: `const` by default, `let` when the value changes, never `var`.
Arrow functions with `map` and `filter` change lists without loops.
Destructuring: `const { title, status } = job;`. Spread copies without changing the original: `{ ...job }`.
Optional chaining `job?.company?.name` and defaults `?? 'none'` avoid crashes.
Modules: `export` shares a value, `import` uses it. Use `"type": "module"` in Node.
asynchronous-javascript-promises-async-a: Slow jobs (network, files) must not freeze JavaScript, so they run asynchronously.
A promise is a placeholder for a value that arrives later.
`await` pauses only your function. Wrap it in `try/catch` to handle failure.
`Promise.all` runs tasks at the same time.
`fetch` returns a promise. Check `response.ok`, then `await response.json()`.
Callbacks are the older way. Prefer async/await.
http-json-and-rest-basics: A request = method + path + headers + sometimes a JSON body.
GET reads, POST creates, PATCH changes, DELETE removes.
Status codes: 2xx success, 4xx the request was wrong, 5xx the server failed.
Common ones: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 400, 401, 404, 500.
REST: nouns in the path (`/api/jobs/12`), verbs in the method.
plan-the-job-tracker-project: Plan before coding: what must people be able to do?
Features become screens, screens become API routes, routes decide the data.
Folders: one for the `server`, one for the `client`.
A plan costs minutes and saves hours of rewriting.
node-js-basics-modules-files-events: Node runs JavaScript on your computer, not in a browser.
Built-in modules: `fs` for files, `path` for file paths, `events` for events.
Use `path.join` so paths work on every system.
An event emitter lets one part announce something and others react.
npm-package-json-and-environment-variabl: `package.json` = name, scripts and the packages the project needs.
`npm install` reads it and fills `node_modules`. Do not commit `node_modules`.
Scripts: `npm run dev` and `npm start`. `nodemon` or `--watch` restarts on change.
Secrets and settings go in `.env`, loaded by `dotenv` into `process.env`. Never commit `.env`.
Commit `.env.example` with the names only, so others know what to fill in.
your-first-express-server-and-routes: Express checks routes from the top and runs the first match.
`res.status(200).json(data)` sends the answer and ends the request.
Order matters: put specific routes before general ones.
Try it with the browser, `curl` or a REST client.
express-middleware-json-cors-and-logging: Middleware = a function every request passes through, in order.
It must call `next()` or send a reply. Otherwise the request hangs.
`express.json()` turns the JSON body into `req.body`. Without it `req.body` is empty.
`cors` lets the browser app call this API.
A logger records method, path and time taken.
Middleware can be added to one route only.
express-routers-and-controllers: Split by responsibility so the project stays readable.
A router lists URLs and the functions that answer them.
A controller holds the logic: read input, do the work, send the reply.
Moving to MongoDB later only changes the data layer.
validation-and-error-handling-in-express: Never trust what a client sends.
Validate: check the types, keep only the allowed fields, clean the text.
One error middleware at the end sends one JSON shape for every error.
Unexpected errors become a plain 500. Details go in the log, not to the visitor.
test-your-api-with-rest-client-and-smoke: Try the routes after writing them.
Level 1: a `.http` file, Postman or `curl`, one request at a time.
Check both the status code and the body.
Level 2: a smoke script repeats all checks so you can run it after every change.
what-is-mongodb-documents-collections-at: A server holds databases, a database holds collections, a collection holds documents.
A document is a JSON-like object with an `_id`.
A collection is like a table, but documents need not have the same fields.
Atlas = MongoDB hosted for you. Or install it locally.
`mongosh` lets you try `insertOne`, `find` and `updateOne` by hand.
connect-express-to-mongodb-with-mongoose: The connection string is a secret: keep it in `.env`.
Start listening only after the database connects.
If it fails, stop with a clear message.
Common problems: wrong password, IP address not allowed in Atlas, special characters in the password.
mongoose-schemas-models-and-validation: A schema describes a document: fields, types, `required`, defaults, allowed values.
`mongoose.model('Job', schema)` gives the tool to read and write jobs.
Bad data is rejected with a `ValidationError`.
`Job.create()` or `save()` writes it to the collection.
crud-with-mongoose-in-express: Create: `Job.create` with only the allowed fields from the body (not the whole `req.body`).
Read one: `Job.findById`. A bad id gives 400, a missing job gives 404.
Update: PATCH with `runValidators: true` so the rules apply to changes too.
Translate database errors into friendly API errors.
search-filter-sort-pagination-and-indexe: The client sends search, status, sort and page in the URL.
Escape search text so it cannot be used as a regex attack.
`skip` and `limit` return one page. Send the total so the client can show page numbers.
Cap the limit so nobody asks for a million rows.
An index lets MongoDB jump to matches instead of reading every document.
mongodb-aggregation-pipeline-for-statist: An aggregation is a pipeline: each stage gets the output of the one before.
`$match` keeps the documents you want, for example the current user's jobs.
`$group` makes buckets, for example by status, and counts them.
Shape the result into a simple object for the dashboard.
Route order matters: `/stats` must come before `/:id`.
user-registration-and-password-hashing-w: Never store passwords. Store a hash.
bcrypt = one-way, adds a random salt, slow on purpose.
Check the email format and a sensible password length first.
A stolen database does not give the passwords away.
The reply never includes the hash.
A duplicate email gives a clear conflict error (409).
login-with-jwt-json-web-tokens: Login: find the user, compare the password with the stored hash using bcrypt.
Unknown email? Compare against a dummy hash anyway, so timing does not reveal which emails exist.
On success sign a JWT with a secret. It holds the user id and an expiry.
The client sends the token with later requests in the `Authorization` header.
Use the same message for every login failure.
Where the client stores the token (memory, localStorage or a cookie) is a security trade-off.
protect-routes-and-ownership-checks: The `protect` middleware reads the token from `Authorization`, verifies it and loads the user.
No token or a bad one: 401. Otherwise set `req.user` and call `next()`.
Every query includes the owner: find by id AND user.
Never take the user id from the request body.
Another person's job gives 404, as if it did not exist, so nothing is leaked.
Prove it with a test: user B cannot read or change user A's data.
express-security-basics-helmet-rate-limi: Security is several small layers, not one switch.
`helmet` adds safe headers to every reply.
Rate limit login routes so nobody can try thousands of passwords.
NoSQL injection sends objects like `{"$gt": ""}` instead of strings. Reject keys that start with `$`.
Behind a proxy set `trust proxy` so the limiter sees the real visitor address.
In production, refuse to start with a missing or weak JWT secret.
automated-api-tests-with-node-test-runne: Tests are code that checks your code. `node --test` needs no extra package.
Split `app.js` (the app) from `server.js` (listening), so tests can import the app without a real server.
Use a separate test database and clear it before each run.
Each test sends a request and checks the status and the body, including failure cases.
Run the tests before every deploy.
react-and-vite-setup-components-and-jsx: A component is a function that returns JSX. Names start with a capital letter.
Vite compiles JSX and reloads instantly while you work.
Components can contain other components, like `Header` and `JobCard`.
A Vite proxy sends `/api` calls to your Express server during development.
react-props-state-and-events: Props: inputs from the parent. They are read-only.
State: data that changes. `const [jobs, setJobs] = useState([])`.
Never change state in place. Make a new array: `[...jobs, newJob]`, `filter`, `map`.
Events: `onClick`, `onChange`. Pass the function, do not call it.
A child tells the parent by calling a function it received as a prop.
Lists need a stable `key`, the id.
react-lists-forms-and-controlled-inputs: Controlled input: state is the single source of truth. `value` shows it, `onChange` updates it.
On submit validate the state first and show clear messages next to the fields.
Every input has a `label` tied to it. It helps screen readers and makes the click area bigger.
Lists use a stable `key`, the id, not the index.
Keep state in the nearest component that needs it, or lift it up.
react-useeffect-and-fetching-data-from-y: Render first with no data and show a loading state. Then the effect starts the fetch.
The dependency list says when to run it again.
Three states: loading, error (with retry), data.
The cleanup function cancels the request, so old answers cannot overwrite new ones.
Keep all API calls in one helper file that adds the token and handles errors.
react-router-pages-links-and-params: The URL decides which page shows. React Router matches it against your routes.
A layout route draws the header once and `<Outlet />` shows the page inside it.
`useParams` reads `:id` from the URL, then load that job.
`Link` and `NavLink` change the URL without reloading.
A `*` route shows a not found page.
react-context-and-custom-hooks: Context shares data (like the signed-in user) without passing props through every level.
A provider holds the data. `useContext` reads it.
A custom hook `useAuth` hides the context behind one call.
`useJobs` keeps loading, error and reload logic in one reusable place.
react-crud-ui-create-edit-delete-with-th: Forms and buttons call the `api` helper, which adds the token and the JSON.
The server validates and changes the data, then replies.
Update the list in state only after the server confirms, using new arrays.
Show a saving state on the button. Confirm before delete.
Show a clear message when a request fails.
sign-in-and-register-pages-with-protecte: `ProtectedRoute` checks the auth context. No user: redirect to login and remember the wanted address.
After login save the token and go back to the page they wanted.
A 401 from the server signs the person out and shows the login page again.
Hiding a page in React is only a convenience. The server still checks every request.
react-dashboard-stats-filters-and-pagina: Put the search, status and page in the URL with `useSearchParams`.
The data hook watches the URL and fetches again when it changes.
The back button, reload and shared links then all work.
Debounce typing so one request is sent, not one per key.
Small focused components: list, stats, pagination.
responsive-styling-and-accessibility-in-: Mobile first: write styles for a small screen, then add `min-width` media queries.
Grid and flexible sizes let cards fill the space without fixed widths.
Visible focus rings, labels, enough colour contrast, keyboard use.
`prefers-color-scheme` gives a dark mode that follows the device.
react-performance-memo-debounce-and-code: Slowness comes from doing too much work, not from React itself.
Debounce: wait until typing stops, then send one request.
`React.memo` skips redrawing a component whose props did not change.
`lazy` loads a page only when it is visited, so the first load is smaller.
Measure first with the browser tools and the build output, then optimise.
file-upload-with-multer-and-react: React sends the file in `FormData`. It checks the size as a courtesy.
`multer` reads the upload with a size limit, one file only and an extension filter.
Read the first bytes: a text file renamed to `.pdf` is rejected and deleted.
Store the file under a random name. Only the details go in MongoDB.
Downloads go through a route that checks ownership and send the file as an attachment.
production-ready-express-logging-gracefu: Log JSON lines with path, status and time. Never log passwords or tokens.
A health check that tests the database. 503 means do not send traffic here.
On `SIGTERM`: stop new connections, finish current requests, close the database, exit.
Build indexes on purpose after a deploy. Compress text responses.
Check the logs when something looks wrong, not only when it breaks.
build-and-serve-the-react-app-from-expre: `npm run build` makes hashed static files in `client/dist`.
Express serves them. Hashed `/assets` are cached for a year. `index.html` is never cached.
`/api` goes to the API. An unknown API path is a JSON 404.
Any other GET returns `index.html`, so React Router works after a reload.
One process and one origin: no CORS needed, one thing to deploy.
deploy-a-mern-app-to-a-vps-with-pm2-ngin: DNS points the name to your server. nginx handles HTTPS (Let's Encrypt) and proxies to Node.
Pass the visitor address in headers and set `trust proxy`.
pm2 keeps the app running, restarts it after a crash and after a reboot.
Settings live in the server's `.env`, never in Git.
A repeatable deploy script: pull, install, build, restart, then check `/api/health`.
Open only the ports you need (80 and 443).
mern-capstone-checklist-and-next-steps: Checklist: secrets, ownership checks, validation, tests, backups, monitoring.
A committed secret stays in Git history. Check it and change the secret.
Deploy, then write a README with screenshots.
Pick one idea from the next-steps list and build it with a test.
Small, finished and deployed projects teach more than unfinished big ones.

what-is-artificial-intelligence: AI = computers doing tasks that normally need human thinking.
Machine learning = learning patterns from examples instead of writing every rule.
Deep learning = machine learning with neural networks of many layers.
Generative AI = creates new text, images or code.
Every system today is narrow AI: very good at some tasks, not a general thinking mind.
AI can be wrong. Check anything that matters.
math-and-statistics-for-ai: A vector = a list of numbers. AI turns words, pictures and data into vectors.
Similarity: how close two vectors are. Search by meaning is built on it.
Probability = how likely each outcome is. A language model scores every possible next word.
Loss = a number for how wrong the model was.
Gradient descent = change the model a little in the direction that lowers the loss, and repeat.
machine-learning-basics: Three ways to learn: supervised (with answers), unsupervised (find groups), reinforcement (rewards).
Split data: training set (learn), validation set (compare settings), test set (final honest check).
Keep the test set locked away until the end.
Overfitting: great training score, poor test score. The model memorised.
Underfitting: the model is too simple to learn the pattern.
Accuracy is not enough. Look at precision and recall too.
deep-learning-and-transformers: A neuron is a small calculator. Many layers learn more complex patterns.
Training: guess, measure the loss, adjust the weights, repeat.
Your words become tokens, then embeddings (lists of numbers carrying meaning).
Attention lets each word look at the others and decide which matter.
At the end the model scores every possible next token and picks one.
introduction-to-generative-ai: Predictive AI picks a label or a number. Generative AI creates new content.
A foundation model is trained once on a very large amount of data and used for many tasks.
Core idea: predict the next piece (word, pixel, sound).
Output can be fluent and still wrong (hallucination).
A person must check anything that matters. Use it responsibly.
how-large-language-models-work: The prompt is split into tokens (words or parts of words).
The context window is how many tokens the model can read at once.
The model scores every possible next token. Sampling picks one.
Low temperature = safest choices. High temperature = more varied.
Each new token is fed back in and the loop repeats.
The model predicts likely text. It does not look facts up, so it can sound sure and be wrong.
llm-architecture-and-optimization: Parameters = the numbers a model learned. Large models have billions.
They take a lot of memory. Memory needed is roughly parameters times bytes per parameter.
Quantization stores numbers with fewer bits: a smaller model, a small loss in quality.
Inference = running the model to answer. GPUs do many calculations in parallel.
Long chats get expensive because the cache and the context grow.
prompt-engineering-basics: Say clearly what the task is. A vague prompt gets a vague answer.
Give a role, the reader and the length.
Add context the model cannot know: your text, data or rules.
A few examples of the exact output teach the format better than a description.
Zero-shot = no examples, one-shot = one, few-shot = several.
Reuse a good prompt as a template with variables.
advanced-prompting-techniques: One huge prompt often gives a messy answer. Split it into steps.
Prompt chaining: the output of one prompt becomes the input of the next.
Ask the model to check its own draft against your rules (reflection).
Pass data between steps in a clear format, for example JSON.
Small steps are easier to test and fix than one giant prompt.
structured-outputs-json: Describe the exact shape you want: field names, types, allowed values.
Never trust the output blindly. Parse and validate every field.
Extract the JSON, check it against the schema, then repair or retry with the error message.
If it still fails, fall back to a safe default.
Only validated data reaches the rest of your app.
prompt-testing-and-security: Build a golden test set: real inputs with the answers you expect.
Save every prompt change as a new version so you can compare and roll back.
A new prompt must not make old cases fail.
Prompt injection = text in a document or message that tries to give the model new orders.
Treat outside text as data, not instructions. Never let the model alone approve risky actions.

what-is-anthropic-and-claude: Claude = a family of AI models made by Anthropic. Use it in the apps or through the API.
In the AI Lab: Angular screen, then your Node.js server, then the Claude API.
The browser never talks to Claude directly.
The server holds the secret API key, so nobody can steal it from the browser.
Choose a model for the task by testing, not by guessing.
set-up-claude-api-key-node: Get an API key from the Anthropic Console.
Put it in `.env`. Never commit it to Git.
The server reads the key from the environment and uses the official SDK.
Angular only talks to your server and never sees the key.
If a key leaks, delete it in the Console at once and create a new one.
Check what comes from the browser and show friendly errors.
claude-api-pricing-limits-tokens: A token is a small piece of text. Everything sent and received is counted in tokens.
Input tokens = what you send. Output tokens = what Claude writes. They are priced differently.
Cost comes from both counts. Check the price list on the Anthropic site, it changes.
Rate limits cap requests or tokens per period. Handle them politely.
Spend less: shorter prompts, trim old history, a smaller model, cache repeated text.
claude-messages-api-explained: Claude has no memory. Every call must carry the whole conversation.
A request has a model, `max_tokens`, a system prompt and a list of messages.
Build and clean the history on the server so a user cannot slip in fake turns.
A longer history means more tokens and a higher cost.
Read the answer from the content blocks, and check `stop_reason`.
stream-claude-responses: Streaming shows words as they are made, so the reader does not wait for the whole answer.
The SDK streams pieces to your server. The server passes them on with Server-Sent Events.
Angular reads the stream and appends each piece to the screen.
A Stop button cancels the request, so you stop paying for text nobody wants.
claude-error-handling-retries: Temporary errors (overload, rate limit) may succeed if you retry.
Errors caused by your own request (wrong key, bad input) will never heal. Fix them.
Exponential backoff: wait longer each time. Add jitter: a little random delay.
The SDK already retries some errors.
Set a timeout and allow cancellation.
Show a clear message. Never show raw error details or secrets.
prompt-caching-and-batch-processing: Same long text again and again wastes tokens.
Put stable text first and mark it for caching. Put the changing question last.
Later requests with the same prefix read from the cache: cheaper and faster.
Check the usage numbers to confirm it works.
A cache expires, and changing even one early word breaks it.
If the answer can wait, the batch API is cheaper.
claude-vision-pdf-documents: Claude can read images and PDFs as well as text.
The server checks file type and size and rejects anything unexpected.
Send the file with a clear question, often asking for JSON. Validate the answer.
Privacy first: do not keep documents longer than needed. Delete the file when done.
Check the size and quality limits in the docs.
claude-tool-use-explained: You describe tools to Claude: a name, what it does, and its inputs.
Claude does not run anything. It replies that it wants to use a tool, with inputs.
Your server runs the tool and sends the result back as a tool result.
Claude writes the final answer from the result.
The loop stops when no more tools are needed.
Tool results are data, not orders.
safe-tool-design-and-permissions: Claude can ask for any tool call, and it can be tricked. Your code is the last line of defence.
Rule 1: validate arguments as if a stranger typed them.
Rule 2: check the signed-in user owns the data.
Rule 3: least privilege, only the access the tool needs.
Rule 4: ask a human before risky actions such as delete or pay.
Rule 5: make actions safe to repeat.
Text returned by a tool is data. It must not change your rules.
build-resume-job-match-with-claude: Plan the exact result first: score, matching skills, missing skills.
The server limits the size and protects the endpoint from abuse.
A forced tool makes Claude return structured JSON.
Still validate the JSON before using it.
A careful system prompt: use only facts given, do not invent.
Show the result as an estimate, not a promise.
prompt-design-for-claude: Write the prompt like a brief for a smart new colleague: task, reason, format.
Use XML tags to separate instructions, documents and the question.
One or two examples of the output teach better than a description.
Long documents go first, the question goes last.
Run the same test cases on every new prompt version.
Do not trust one lucky answer.

what-is-rag: A model only knows what it was trained on. RAG gives it your documents at question time.
Steps: question, search your documents, add the best passages to the prompt, the model answers from them, with sources.
Tell the model to answer only from the passages and to say so when they do not contain the answer.
RAG is not magic: if the search finds the wrong passages, the answer will be wrong too.
chunking-embeddings-vector-search: Parse and clean documents first so only useful text remains.
Chunking: small enough to be focused, big enough to make sense alone.
Overlap between chunks protects the borders.
An embedding = a list of numbers that captures meaning.
Store embeddings in a vector index with the text and its source.
Embed the question the same way and find the closest chunks (cosine similarity).
vector-databases-explained: A vector database stores embeddings and finds the nearest ones fast.
Exact search is slower. Approximate search is faster with a small loss.
Metadata filters, for example by permission, stop one user seeing another user's documents.
Options: pgvector, Qdrant, Pinecone, Chroma. Start simple.
Put the database behind an interface so you can change it later.
advanced-rag-and-evaluation: One search method is not enough. Hybrid search = keywords (BM25) plus meaning (vectors).
Reciprocal Rank Fusion merges two rankings into one list.
A similarity threshold lets the system say nothing relevant was found.
A reranker reads each candidate with the question and puts the best first.
Citations let the reader check the source. The server should check them.
Measure retrieval with real questions: did the right passage appear in the top results?
ai-agents-explained: An agent is given a goal, not a single question.
Loop: think, act (call a tool), observe, check if the goal is reached, repeat.
Put limits on the loop: a step limit and a budget.
Keep tools small and clear. Ask a person before risky actions.
Agents can fail in ways a single answer cannot.
multi-agent-systems-and-frameworks: Multi-agent = several agents, each with a focused job and its own instructions.
A lead agent splits the task. A checker agent reviews the result.
More agents mean more cost, more delay and more that can go wrong.
Add them only when one agent is not enough.
Frameworks and the Claude Agent SDK help, but check the current docs.
what-is-mcp-model-context-protocol: MCP = a standard way to connect an AI app to tools and data.
Three roles: host (the app with the model), client (inside the host), server (offers the tools).
A server can offer tools, resources and prompts.
The client asks what is available, then calls one.
One standard replaces a custom connection for every app and tool.
The MCP Inspector helps you debug a server.
build-an-mcp-server-node: Install the MCP SDK and register a tool with a name, a description and an input schema.
Test it with the MCP Inspector before connecting any AI app.
The host starts your server and talks to it over a local connection.
Good tools: clear descriptions, validated inputs, small and one job each.
Two kinds of failure: a protocol error and a tool that ran but failed. Report both clearly.
mcp-security-and-integration: An MCP server can touch real systems. Every connection is a security decision.
Least privilege: for example read-only access.
Ask the user to approve actions that change things or send data out.
Check who is asking and what they are allowed to do.
Tool results are untrusted text. They may hide instructions meant to trick the model.
evaluating-llm-applications: "It seems to work" is not enough.
Write a golden set: real questions and what a good answer looks like.
Score with code rules, an AI judge or people. An AI judge has limits.
Also measure cost, speed and safety.
Run the same tests on every change.
ai-safety-privacy-and-responsible-ai: Risk: wrong answers that sound right. Ground answers in sources and check them.
Risk: personal data leaving your system. Send only what the task needs.
Check your provider's terms and keep your promises to users.
Risk: unfairness. A person must make the final call on hiring, health and money decisions.
Go through a checklist before you launch an AI feature.
running-ai-in-production: Plan cost, reliability and monitoring from day one.
Before the model call: rate limit, budget and cache.
Use timeouts, retries and a fallback if the model is unavailable.
Monitor cost, errors, slow answers and quality. Alert when they change.
Release slowly and keep a way to roll back.
When something breaks: follow an incident plan, fix the cause, add a test.
ai-learning-roadmap-and-projects: Basics first: what AI, machine learning and language models are.
Then build with the API: messages, streaming, errors, tools.
Then your own data and actions: RAG, agents, MCP.
Practise with small projects and keep improving them.
Building is how the ideas stick.
